description: 200 questions on Python string methods (coding questions, beginner to intermediate)

questions.question: What does 'Hello'.upper() return?
questions.answer:
.upper() converts every letter to uppercase, so 'Hello' becomes 'HELLO'.

code:
print('Hello'.upper())  # HELLO

real example:
Shouting a headline or normalising product names.

questions.question: What does 'Hello'.lower() return?
questions.answer:
.lower() converts every letter to lowercase, so 'Hello' becomes 'hello'.

code:
print('Hello'.lower())  # hello

real example:
Making search keywords lowercase so they match reliably.

questions.question: What does 'hELLO wORLD'.capitalize() return?
questions.answer:
.capitalize() uppercases only the first letter and lowercases everything else.

code:
print('hELLO wORLD'.capitalize())  # Hello world

real example:
Fixing a sentence typed in all caps to normal sentence case.

questions.question: What does 'hello world'.title() return?
questions.answer:
.title() capitalises the first letter of every word and lowercases the rest.

code:
print('hello world'.title())  # Hello World

real example:
Converting a lowercase book title into Title Case.

questions.question: What does 'Hello'.swapcase() return?
questions.answer:
.swapcase() flips each letter's case: upper becomes lower and vice versa.

code:
print('Hello'.swapcase())  # hELLO

real example:
Quickly inverting the case of a previously capitalised code.

questions.question: What does 'ß'.upper() return?
questions.answer:
The German sharp-s ß uppercases unusually to two letters, 'SS'.

code:
print('ß'.upper())  # SS

real example:
Handling international text where one letter can grow to two.

questions.question: What does 'PYTHON'.lower() return?
questions.answer:
.lower() converts all letters to lowercase, turning 'PYTHON' into 'python'.

code:
print('PYTHON'.lower())  # python

real example:
Storing user input in lowercase for consistent matching.

questions.question: What does 'aBc'.swapcase() return?
questions.answer:
.swapcase() swaps each letter's case: 'aBc' becomes 'AbC'.

code:
print('aBc'.swapcase())  # AbC

real example:
Flipping case in a playful name style.

questions.question: What does 'media'.casefold() return?
questions.answer:
.casefold() makes text lowercase, so 'media' stays 'media', and it also handles special letters more aggressively than lower().

code:
print('media'.casefold())  # media

real example:
Comparing usernames ignoring case across languages.

questions.question: What does '123abc'.upper() return?
questions.answer:
.upper() changes only letters; digits pass through unchanged, so '123abc' becomes '123ABC'.

code:
print('123abc'.upper())  # 123ABC

real example:
Uppercasing an alphanumeric reference code.

questions.question: What does 'one two three'.title() return?
questions.answer:
.title() capitalises the first letter of each word: One, Two, Three.

code:
print('one two three'.title())  # One Two Three

real example:
Formatting a list of items as a proper heading.

questions.question: What does 'hello'.upper().lower() return?
questions.answer:
.upper() makes 'HELLO' and then .lower() lowers it again, returning to the original 'hello'.

code:
print('hello'.upper().lower())  # hello

real example:
Chaining methods when both cleanups run in sequence.

questions.question: What does '  hi  '.capitalize() return?
questions.answer:
.capitalize() changes only the first letter's case; leading and trailing spaces are kept.

code:
print(repr('  hi  '.capitalize()))  # '  hi  '

real example:
Capitalising content of a field while preserving its padding.

questions.question: What does 'a1b2'.upper() return?
questions.answer:
.upper() only affects letters, so 'a1b2' becomes 'A1B2' with digits unchanged.

code:
print('a1b2'.upper())  # A1B2

real example:
Uppercasing a code that mixes letters and numbers.

questions.question: What does 'PYTHON'.isupper() return?
questions.answer:
.isupper() returns True when there is at least one letter and every letter is uppercase.

code:
print('PYTHON'.isupper())  # True

real example:
Checking whether a flag or label is in shout form.

questions.question: What does 'Python'.isupper() return?
questions.answer:
.isupper() is False because 'Python' has lowercase letters too.

code:
print('Python'.isupper())  # False

real example:
Verifying that input is not mixed-case before processing.

questions.question: What does 'python'.islower() return?
questions.answer:
.islower() returns True when every cased letter is lowercase, and 'python' qualifies.

code:
print('python'.islower())  # True

real example:
Confirming text uses only small letters.

questions.question: What does 'Hello World'.istitle() return?
questions.answer:
.istitle() checks that each word starts with an uppercase letter and the rest are lowercase.

code:
print('Hello World'.istitle())  # True

real example:
Verifying a heading follows Title Case rules.

questions.question: What does 'hello world'.istitle() return?
questions.answer:
.istitle() needs capitals at each word start; 'hello world' has none, so it is False.

code:
print('hello world'.istitle())  # False

real example:
Checking whether a label was already title-cased.

questions.question: What does 'country's title method do for a one-word lowercase string?
questions.answer:
.title() on a one-word lowercase string capitalises just its first letter.

code:
print('country'.title())  # Country

real example:
Converting a single lowercase word into a proper noun.

questions.question: Which method is best for case-insensitive comparisons?
questions.answer:
casefold() is best because it handles more letters (like ß) for genuine case-insensitive comparisons.

code:
print('STRASSE'.casefold() == 'strasse'.casefold())  # True

real example:
Matching city names or words regardless of letter case.

questions.question: What does 'HELLO there'.swapcase() return?
questions.answer:
.swapcase() flips every letter, turning 'HELLO there' into 'hello THERE'.

code:
print('HELLO there'.swapcase())  # hello THERE

real example:
Inverting case for a stylised heading.

questions.question: What does '  hello  '.strip() return?
questions.answer:
.strip() removes whitespace from both ends, so '  hello  ' becomes 'hello'.

code:
print('  hello  '.strip())  # hello

real example:
Cleaning extra spaces pasted around user input.

questions.question: What does '  hello  '.lstrip() return?
questions.answer:
.lstrip() removes whitespace only from the left side, keeping the right-side spaces.

code:
print(repr('  hello  '.lstrip()))  # 'hello  '

real example:
Trimming accidental indent from the start of pasted text.

questions.question: What does '  hello  '.rstrip() return?
questions.answer:
.rstrip() removes whitespace only from the right side, keeping the leading spaces.

code:
print(repr('  hello  '.rstrip()))  # '  hello'

real example:
Removing trailing spaces at the end of a line of text.

questions.question: What does '.-hello-.'.strip('.-') return?
questions.answer:
strip('.-') removes any of the given characters from both ends, so the surrounding dots and dashes fall away.

code:
print('.-hello-.'.strip('.-'))  # hello

real example:
Cleaning punctuation and dashes off a quoted value.

questions.question: What does 'abcabcx'.strip('abc') return?
questions.answer:
strip('abc') strips any 'a', 'b', or 'c' characters from both ends, leaving only 'x' in the middle.

code:
print('abcabcx'.strip('abc'))  # x

real example:
Removing wrapper letters around a coded value.

questions.question: What does 'xabc'.strip('x') return?
questions.answer:
strip('x') removes 'x' from the start, leaving the rest of the string 'abc'.

code:
print('xabc'.strip('x'))  # abc

real example:
Stripping a single leading marker character.

questions.question: What does 'aaa'.strip('a') return?
questions.answer:
Every character is 'a', so stripping 'a' removes everything and the result is an empty string.

code:
print(repr('aaa'.strip('a')))  # ''

real example:
Handling strings that are entirely made of the stripped characters.

questions.question: What does 'hello'.strip() return?
questions.answer:
'hello' has no surrounding whitespace, so strip() returns it unchanged.

code:
print('hello'.strip())  # hello

real example:
A safe cleanup that leaves already-clean text alone.

questions.question: What does '\t hi \t'.strip() return?
questions.answer:
strip() removes tabs too, so the tabs around ' hi ' are gone and only 'hi' remains.

code:
print(repr('\t hi \t'.strip()))  # 'hi'

real example:
Cleaning a value pasted from a spreadsheet that used tabs.

questions.question: What does '\nhello\n'.strip() return?
questions.answer:
strip() removes newline characters, so the newlines around 'hello' are dropped.

code:
print(repr('\nhello\n'.strip()))  # 'hello'

real example:
Cleaning a line read from a file that ends with a newline.

questions.question: What does strip() remove by default?
questions.answer:
By default, strip() removes whitespace: spaces, tabs, and newline characters.

code:
print(repr(' \t\n '.strip()))  # ''

real example:
Sanitising free-form input that may contain blank spaces.

questions.question: What does 'abab'.strip('ab') return?
questions.answer:
Every character is either 'a' or 'b', so strip('ab') removes all of them, leaving nothing.

code:
print(repr('abab'.strip('ab')))  # ''

real example:
A pattern that is fully consumed by its own wrapper characters.

questions.question: What does '--==--'.strip('-=') return?
questions.answer:
Both characters '-' and '=' form the whole string, so stripping removes everything.

code:
print(repr('--==--'.strip('-=')))  # ''

real example:
Checking whether a decorative border is entirely wrappers.

questions.question: What does 'python'.strip('pn') return?
questions.answer:
strip('pn') removes 'p' from the front and 'n' from the back, leaving the middle 'ytho'.

code:
print('python'.strip('pn'))  # ytho

real example:
Stripping a leading and trailing letter from a word code.

questions.question: What does 'coconut'.strip('co') return?
questions.answer:
strip('co') removes 'c' and 'o' from the ends, so 'coconut' turns into 'nut'.

code:
print('coconut'.strip('co'))  # nut

real example:
Removing wrapper letters from a phrase code.

questions.question: What does '  hello world  '.strip() return?
questions.answer:
strip() with no argument removes the surrounding spaces, keeping the inner space between the words.

code:
print('  hello world  '.strip())  # hello world

real example:
Cleaning whitespace from pasted sentences.

questions.question: What does '###head###'.strip('#') return?
questions.answer:
strip('#') removes the hash characters from both ends, exposing 'head' in the middle.

code:
print('###head###'.strip('#'))  # head

real example:
Removing markdown-style bold markers around a word.

questions.question: What does '0GOOD0'.strip('0') return?
questions.answer:
strip('0') removes the zeros from both ends, leaving the inner text 'GOOD'.

code:
print('0GOOD0'.strip('0'))  # GOOD

real example:
Dropping padding zeros around a stored code.

questions.question: What does 'bat'.strip('tab') return?
questions.answer:
'bat' is made entirely of 't', 'a', and 'b', so stripping those removes the whole word.

code:
print(repr('bat'.strip('tab')))  # ''

real example:
A word that happens to be built only from wrapper letters.

questions.question: What does '   '.strip() return?
questions.answer:
The string is nothing but spaces, so stripping whitespace removes every character.

code:
print(repr('   '.strip()))  # ''

real example:
Identifying input that is only blank spaces.

questions.question: What does 'a b'.rstrip('b') return?
questions.answer:
rstrip('b') removes 'b' only from the right side, leaving the trailing space before it.

code:
print(repr('a b'.rstrip('b')))  # 'a '

real example:
Removing a trailing letter while keeping the space.

questions.question: What does ' a'.lstrip() return?
questions.answer:
.lstrip() removes the leading space, so ' a' becomes 'a'.

code:
print(' a'.lstrip())  # a

real example:
Cleaning a stray leading space in pasted input.

questions.question: What does 'hello'.find('l') return?
questions.answer:
.find('l') scans from the start and returns the first index where 'l' appears, which is 2.

code:
print('hello'.find('l'))  # 2

real example:
Locating the first occurrence of a letter for highlighting.

questions.question: What does 'hello'.find('l', 3) return?
questions.answer:
.find('l', 3) starts searching at index 3, so it finds the second 'l' there.

code:
print('hello'.find('l', 3))  # 3

real example:
Finding a later occurrence after a chosen starting point.

questions.question: What does 'hello'.find('z') return?
questions.answer:
.find('z') returns -1 when the text is not found, instead of raising an error.

code:
print('hello'.find('z'))  # -1

real example:
Checking whether a value like 'z' exists in user input.

questions.question: What does 'hello'.index('l') return?
questions.answer:
.index('l') also returns the first index, and here 'l' first occurs at 2.

code:
print('hello'.index('l'))  # 2

real example:
Getting the position of a letter you know must be present.

questions.question: What does 'hello'.index('z') do?
questions.answer:
.index('z') raises a ValueError because 'z' is not found, unlike find which returns -1.

code:
# 'hello'.index('z')  # ValueError: substring not found

real example:
Using .find instead when a missing value should be handled gently.

questions.question: What does 'ababa'.count('a') return?
questions.answer:
.count('a') counts non-overlapping occurrences of 'a', and 'ababa' has three of them.

code:
print('ababa'.count('a'))  # 3

real example:
Counting how often a chosen letter appears in a word.

questions.question: What does 'ababa'.count('aba') return?
questions.answer:
count() counts non-overlapping matches; 'aba' matches once at the start, leaving no second occurrence.

code:
print('ababa'.count('aba'))  # 1

real example:
Counting how many whole words appear without double-counting overlaps.

questions.question: What does 'aaaa'.count('aa') return?
questions.answer:
count() does not overlap: 'aaaa' finds 'aa' at 0-1 and again at 2-3, so the total is 2.

code:
print('aaaa'.count('aa'))  # 2

real example:
Counting pairs in a repeated-code string without overlap.

questions.question: What does 'banana'.count('na') return?
questions.answer:
'na' appears twice in 'banana': at index 2 and at index 4, so count returns 2.

code:
print('banana'.count('na'))  # 2

real example:
Counting syllables or letter pairs in a word.

questions.question: What does 'batman'.find('man') return?
questions.answer:
.find('man') returns the starting index of 'man', which here is 3.

code:
print('batman'.find('man'))  # 3

real example:
Finding where a substring begins in a phrase.

questions.question: What does 'hello'.rfind('l') return?
questions.answer:
.rfind('l') searches from the end and returns the last occurrence, which is at index 3.

code:
print('hello'.rfind('l'))  # 3

real example:
Finding the second (rightmost) occurrence of a letter.

questions.question: What does 'hello'.rindex('l') return?
questions.answer:
.rindex('l') also finds the rightmost occurrence, which is the last 'l' at index 3.

code:
print('hello'.rindex('l'))  # 3

real example:
Locating the last matching letter when it must be present.

questions.question: What does 'hello'.rfind('z') return?
questions.answer:
.rfind('z') returns -1 because 'z' does not appear anywhere, just like find.

code:
print('hello'.rfind('z'))  # -1

real example:
A gentle right-to-left search that never crashes on a miss.

questions.question: What does 'test'.find('t', 1) return?
questions.answer:
.find('t', 1) skips the first character, so it finds the second 't' in 'test' at index 3.

code:
print('test'.find('t', 1))  # 3

real example:
Ignoring the first occurrence and finding the next one.

questions.question: How are find() and index() different?
questions.answer:
Both find a substring, but find() returns -1 if missing while index() raises a ValueError instead.

code:
print('hi'.find('z'))  # -1
# 'hi'.index('z')  # ValueError

real example:
Choosing find() when a missing match should be a non-error answer.

questions.question: What does 'mississippi'.count('s') return?
questions.answer:
.count('s') counts the 's' characters in 'mississippi', which appear four times.

code:
print('mississippi'.count('s'))  # 4

real example:
Tallying a letter in a tongue-twister word.

questions.question: What does 'mississippi'.count('iss') return?
questions.answer:
.count('iss') finds non-overlapping matches; 'mississippi' has 'iss' at indexes 1 and 4, so 2.

code:
print('mississippi'.count('iss'))  # 2

real example:
Counting how many times a letter pair-plus appears.

questions.question: What does 'mississippi'.find('ss') return?
questions.answer:
.find('ss') finds the first 'ss'; in 'mississippi' the first one starts at index 2.

code:
print('mississippi'.find('ss'))  # 2

real example:
Locating the first double-letter in a word.

questions.question: What does 'mississippi'.rfind('ss') return?
questions.answer:
.rfind('ss') finds the rightmost 'ss' pair, which starts at index 5.

code:
print('mississippi'.rfind('ss'))  # 5

real example:
Finding the last double-letter when a word has two.

questions.question: What does 'a-b-c'.count('-') return?
questions.answer:
.count('-') counts the dash separators, and 'a-b-c' has two of them.

code:
print('a-b-c'.count('-'))  # 2

real example:
Measuring how many separators a joined string has.

questions.question: What does 'hello world'.find(' ') return?
questions.answer:
.find(' ') returns the index of the first space, which in 'hello world' is 5.

code:
print('hello world'.find(' '))  # 5

real example:
Splitting a sentence at its first space by finding its position.

questions.question: What does 'hello world'.find('o', 5) return?
questions.answer:
.find('o', 5) starts at index 5, so it skips the 'o' in 'hello' and finds the 'o' in 'world' at 7.

code:
print('hello world'.find('o', 5))  # 7

real example:
Searching for a letter after a chosen position.

questions.question: What does 'hello'.find('o') return?
questions.answer:
.find('o') finds the first 'o', which sits at index 4 in 'hello'.

code:
print('hello'.find('o'))  # 4

real example:
Locating a vowel to split a word in half.

questions.question: What does 'geeks'.rfind('e') return?
questions.answer:
.rfind('e') finds the rightmost 'e'; in 'geeks' the last 'e' is at index 2.

code:
print('geeks'.rfind('e'))  # 2

real example:
Finding the final occurrence of a letter in a word.

questions.question: What does 'hello'.replace('l', 'L') return?
questions.answer:
.replace('l', 'L') swaps every 'l' for an uppercase 'L', giving 'heLLo'.

code:
print('hello'.replace('l', 'L'))  # heLLo

real example:
Highlighting a letter in a word-cleanup tool.

questions.question: What does 'banana'.replace('a', 'o') return?
questions.answer:
.replace('a', 'o') changes every 'a' to 'o', so 'banana' becomes 'bonono'.

code:
print('banana'.replace('a', 'o'))  # bonono

real example:
Correcting a repeated typo throughout a word.

questions.question: What does 'aaa'.replace('a', 'b') return?
questions.answer:
.replace('a', 'b') swaps all matches, turning all three 'a's into 'b's.

code:
print('aaa'.replace('a', 'b'))  # bbb

real example:
Renaming every occurrence of a character in a code.

questions.question: What does 'aaa'.replace('a', 'b', 1) return?
questions.answer:
.replace with a count of 1 changes only the first match, leaving the rest alone.

code:
print('aaa'.replace('a', 'b', 1))  # baa

real example:
Fixing the first typo in a line but not later ones.

questions.question: What does 'aaa'.replace('a', 'b', 2) return?
questions.answer:
.replace with a count of 2 changes the first two matches, producing 'bba'.

code:
print('aaa'.replace('a', 'b', 2))  # bba

real example:
Correcting just the first two instances in editing text.

questions.question: What does 'hello'.replace('x', 'y') return?
questions.answer:
When no match exists, replace() returns the original string unchanged.

code:
print('hello'.replace('x', 'y'))  # hello

real example:
A safe edit operation that does nothing on a miss.

questions.question: What does 'hello hello'.replace('hello', 'Hi') return?
questions.answer:
.replace() with no count swaps every occurrence, so both 'hello' words become 'Hi'.

code:
print('hello hello'.replace('hello', 'Hi'))  # Hi Hi

real example:
Renaming every instance of a word in a greeting line.

questions.question: What does 'hello hello'.replace('hello', 'Hi', 1) return?
questions.answer:
A count of 1 changes only the first 'hello', so the second one stays untouched.

code:
print('hello hello'.replace('hello', 'Hi', 1))  # Hi hello

real example:
Renaming just the first occurrence of a repeated word.

questions.question: What does 'hello'.replace('l', '') return?
questions.answer:
replace('l', '') deletes every 'l' by swapping it for nothing, giving 'heo'.

code:
print('hello'.replace('l', ''))  # heo

real example:
Removing a character everywhere in a cleaned phrase.

questions.question: What does 'a.b.c'.replace('.', '-') return?
questions.answer:
.replace('.', '-') swaps all dots for dashes, turning 'a.b.c' into 'a-b-c'.

code:
print('a.b.c'.replace('.', '-'))  # a-b-c

real example:
Converting dotted version numbers to dash-separated ones.

questions.question: What does 'AAA'.replace('a', 'b') return?
questions.answer:
replace() is case-sensitive, and 'AAA' has no lowercase 'a' to match.

code:
print('AAA'.replace('a', 'b'))  # AAA

real example:
Remembering to lowercase both sides before case-fixing text.

questions.question: What does ''.replace('', 'x') return?
questions.answer:
Replacing the empty string inserts the replacement at the single gap, so '' becomes 'x'.

code:
print(repr(''.replace('', 'x')))  # 'x'

real example:
An edge case for inserting text into an empty placeholder.

questions.question: Does replace modify the original string?
questions.answer:
replace() returns a brand-new string; the original string is never modified.

code:
s = 'abc'
s.replace('a', 'z')
print(s)  # abc

real example:
Editing displayed text while keeping the stored original safe.

questions.question: What does 'aA'.lower().replace('a', 'b') return?
questions.answer:
'aA'.lower() gives 'aa', then replace('a', 'b') turns both into 'bb'.

code:
print('aA'.lower().replace('a', 'b'))  # bb

real example:
Case-insensitive find-and-replace inside a search tool.

questions.question: What does 'a,b,c'.split(',') return?
questions.answer:
.split(',') cuts the string at each comma, returning the pieces as a list.

code:
print('a,b,c'.split(','))  # ['a', 'b', 'c']

real example:
Parsing comma-separated values from a simple line.

questions.question: What does 'hello world'.split() return?
questions.answer:
.split() with no separator splits on any whitespace, giving separate words.

code:
print('hello world'.split())  # ['hello', 'world']

real example:
Breaking a sentence into a list of words.

questions.question: What does '  a  b  '.split() return?
questions.answer:
split() with no argument collapses runs of whitespace, so extra spaces are ignored.

code:
print('  a  b  '.split())  # ['a', 'b']

real example:
Cleaning messy, multiply-spaced input into tokens.

questions.question: What does 'abc'.split() return?
questions.answer:
With no spaces to split on, split() returns the whole string as a single-element list.

code:
print('abc'.split())  # ['abc']

real example:
Handling a word-only input in a tokeniser.

questions.question: What does 'a,b,,c'.split(',') return?
questions.answer:
Splitting on ',' keeps empty pieces where two commas touch, so an empty string appears.

code:
print('a,b,,c'.split(','))  # ['a', 'b', '', 'c']

real example:
Parsing CSV rows where blank fields must be preserved.

questions.question: What does 'a b c'.split(' ', 1) return?
questions.answer:
.split(' ', 1) splits only once, so everything after the first space stays whole.

code:
print('a b c'.split(' ', 1))  # ['a', 'b c']

real example:
Separating a command word from the rest of an instruction.

questions.question: What does 'one two three'.split(' ', 2) return?
questions.answer:
Splitting twice with ' ' separates the first two words and keeps the third as one piece.

code:
print('one two three'.split(' ', 2))  # ['one', 'two', 'three']

real example:
Breaking a line into at most three fixed parts.

questions.question: What does 'a-b-c'.rsplit('-', 1) return?
questions.answer:
.rsplit('-', 1) splits from the right, separating only the final field.

code:
print('a-b-c'.rsplit('-', 1))  # ['a-b', 'c']

real example:
Extracting just the last part of a hyphenated code.

questions.question: What does 'a-b-c'.rsplit('-', 2) return?
questions.answer:
.rsplit('-', 2) splits from the right twice, producing all three parts.

code:
print('a-b-c'.rsplit('-', 2))  # ['a', 'b', 'c']

real example:
Decomposing a version string into all of its fields.

questions.question: What does 'a\nb\n'.splitlines() return?
questions.answer:
.splitlines() breaks on newline characters and leaves them out.

code:
print('a\nb\n'.splitlines())  # ['a', 'b']

real example:
Reading lines of a text file into a list.

questions.question: What does 'a\nb\n'.splitlines(keepends=True) return?
questions.answer:
With keepends=True, the newline characters stay attached to each line.

code:
print('a\nb\n'.splitlines(True))  # ['a\n', 'b\n']

real example:
Splitting file text while remembering the line breaks.

questions.question: What does 'hello'.split('l') return?
questions.answer:
.split('l') cuts at each 'l', producing an empty string where two 'l's are adjacent.

code:
print('hello'.split('l'))  # ['he', '', 'o']

"1" maps to "a" and "2" to "b", while x and y stay unchanged, giving 'xayb'.

code:
print('x1y2'.translate(str.maketrans('1234', 'abcd')))  # xayb

real example:
Converting certain digits to letters in a serial code.

questions.question: How do you convert a string to bytes?
questions.answer:
Use s.encode('utf-8') to turn the string into a bytes object encoded in UTF-8.

code:
print('hi'.encode('utf-8'))  # b'hi'

real example:
Preparing text for writing to a binary file.

questions.question: What does 'hi'.encode() return?
questions.answer:
.encode() with the default UTF-8 encoding turns 'hi' into the bytes object b'hi'.

code:
print('hi'.encode())  # b'hi'

real example:
Converting text to the bytes a network socket expects.

questions.question: What does b'hi'.decode() return?
questions.answer:
.decode() turns bytes back into a normal string, so b'hi' becomes 'hi'.

code:
print(b'hi'.decode())  # hi

real example:
Reading bytes from a file and converting to readable text.

questions.question: What is len('é'.encode('utf-8'))?
questions.answer:
In UTF-8, the single character é takes two bytes, so the encoded size is 2.

code:
print(len('é'.encode('utf-8')))  # 2

real example:
Estimating byte sizes when transmitting strings.

questions.question: What does 'A'.encode('ascii') return?
questions.answer:
.encode('ascii') works for characters in the ASCII range, so 'A' becomes b'A'.

code:
print('A'.encode('ascii'))  # b'A'

real example:
Encoding simple text for older ASCII-only channels.

questions.question: What happens encoding 'é' as ASCII?
questions.answer:
é is not an ASCII character, so encoding it that way raises a UnicodeEncodeError.

code:
# 'é'.encode('ascii')  # UnicodeEncodeError

real example:
Handling characters that older encodings simply cannot store.

questions.question: What does 'é'.encode('utf-8') return?
questions.answer:
UTF-8 encodes 'é' as the two bytes \xc3\xa9.

code:
print('é'.encode('utf-8'))  # b'\xc3\xa9'

real example:
Seeing how accented letters appear at the byte level.

questions.question: What does b'\xe9'.decode('latin-1') return?
questions.answer:
Decoding the byte \xe9 with latin-1 produces the character 'é'.

code:
print(b'\xe9'.decode('latin-1'))  # é

real example:
Reading legacy latin-1 text from older databases.

questions.question: What does ''.encode() return?
questions.answer:
Encoding an empty string gives an empty bytes object b''.

code:
print(''.encode())  # b''

real example:
A safe starting point when no text is present to send.

questions.question: What does '123'.encode().decode() return?
questions.answer:
Encoding to bytes and decoding back returns the original text unchanged.

code:
print('123'.encode().decode())  # 123

real example:
Sending text through a binary medium and recovering it.

questions.question: What is the type of 'hi'.encode()?
questions.answer:
The result of 'hi'.encode() has the type bytes.

code:
print(type('hi'.encode()))  # <class 'bytes'>

real example:
Knowing the type when passing data to binary APIs.

questions.question: How do you ignore characters that cannot be encoded?
questions.answer:
The errors='ignore' option skips unencodable characters instead of failing.

code:
print('café'.encode('ascii', errors='ignore'))  # b'caf'

real example:
Sanitising text for systems that only accept ASCII.
